title: Θεῶν ἀγορά
about: The poem opens by asking the Muse to tell of a man who wandered far after the sack of Troy and who could not save his companions, because they ate the cattle of the Sun. The story then begins late: every other survivor of the war is home, and Odysseus alone is held on an island by the nymph Calypso. While Poseidon, his enemy, is away feasting among the Ethiopians, the other gods meet in the hall of Zeus. Zeus reflects on Aegisthus, who was warned and still earned his death. Athena turns the talk to Odysseus. Zeus explains Poseidon's anger over the blinded Cyclops and agrees that Odysseus must come home, and Athena proposes sending Hermes to Calypso while she herself goes to Ithaca to rouse his son.

sentences.t:
ἄνδρα μοι ἔννεπε, μοῦσα, πολύτροπον, ὃς μάλα πολλὰ
πλάγχθη, ἐπεὶ Τροίης ἱερὸν πτολίεθρον ἔπερσεν·
sentences.l:
The man to me tell-of, Muse, the many-turning, who very much
was driven-astray, after Troy's holy citadel he sacked;
sentences.i: Muse, tell me of the man of many shifts, who was driven far off his course after he had sacked the holy citadel of Troy.
sentences.n: ἄνδρα is the poem's first word and its subject; the man is not named until line 21. ἔννεπε is the imperative of ἐννέπω 'tell of'. πολύτροπον has been disputed since antiquity: 'much turned', that is much travelled, or 'of many turns', that is versatile and wily. The relative clause that follows favours the first sense without excluding the second. πλάγχθη is the aorist passive of πλάζω 'drive off course', with no augment: Homer's past tenses may drop the ἐ-, and you will see this constantly. Τροίης has Ionic η where Attic has long α. πτολίεθρον 'citadel, town' is an epic derivative of πτόλις, the old by-form of πόλις.

sentences.t:
πολλῶν δ’ ἀνθρώπων ἴδεν ἄστεα καὶ νόον ἔγνω,
πολλὰ δ’ ὅ γ’ ἐν πόντῳ πάθεν ἄλγεα ὃν κατὰ θυμόν,
ἀρνύμενος ἥν τε ψυχὴν καὶ νόστον ἑταίρων.
sentences.l:
and of many men he saw the towns and their mind came-to-know,
and many, he, on the open-sea suffered pains in his own heart,
striving-to-win both his own life and the homecoming of his companions.
sentences.i: He saw the towns of many peoples and learned how they thought, and out on the sea he bore many pains in his own heart, trying to secure his own life and his companions' homecoming.
sentences.n: πολλά closes line 1, and πολλῶν and πολλά open lines 3 and 4: the word is heard three times in four lines. ἴδεν and πάθεν are unaugmented aorists (Attic εἶδεν, ἔπαθεν). ὅ γε is 'he': what looks like the article is in Homer a pronoun, a pattern that recurs constantly. ὃν κατὰ θυμόν is 'in his own heart': ὅς, ἥ, ὅν is here the possessive adjective 'his own', which is easily mistaken for the relative pronoun. ἥν τε ψυχήν in the next line is the same possessive. ἀρνύμενος means 'striving to win', with both accusatives as its objects. νόστος 'homecoming' appears here for the first time.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ οὐδ’ ὣς ἑτάρους ἐρρύσατο, ἱέμενός περ·
sentences.l: But not even so his companions did he rescue, eager though he was;
sentences.i: Yet even so he did not save his companions, much as he wished to.
sentences.n: οὐδ’ ὥς is 'not even so': accented ὥς is the adverb 'thus' (Attic οὕτως), distinct from unaccented ὡς 'as'. ἑτάρους stands beside ἑταίρων in the line before; the two forms of the word are alternatives that suit different places in the verse. ἐρρύσατο is the aorist middle of ἐρύομαι 'protect, rescue'. ἱέμενος, the middle participle of ἵημι, means 'pressing forward, eager'. περ attached to a participle gives it concessive force, where Attic would use καίπερ.

sentences.t:
αὐτῶν γὰρ σφετέρῃσιν ἀτασθαλίῃσιν ὄλοντο,
νήπιοι, οἳ κατὰ βοῦς Ὑπερίονος Ἠελίοιο
ἤσθιον·
sentences.i: For they perished through their own wanton folly, the fools, who ate up the cattle of Hyperion the Sun;
sentences.n: ἀτασθαλίῃσιν is a dative plural in -ῃσι(ν), Attic -αις; the long dative endings -ῃσι, -οισι, -εσσι are everywhere in Homer. The word returns at 1.34 in the mouth of Zeus. αὐτῶν reinforces σφετέρῃσιν: 'their own, and no one else's'. ὄλοντο is the unaugmented aorist middle of ὄλλυμι. νήπιοι stands first in its line, a judgment on the men before the relative clause explains it. κατὰ … ἤσθιον is tmesis: the preverb stands apart from its verb, and together they are κατήσθιον 'devoured'. Ἠελίοιο is a genitive in -οιο (Attic Ἡλίου). Hyperion is here a name of the Sun himself. His herds were sacred, and the companions killed and ate them.

sentences.t: αὐτὰρ ὁ τοῖσιν ἀφείλετο νόστιμον ἦμαρ.
sentences.l: but he from them took-away the homecoming day.
sentences.i: and he took from them the day of their homecoming.
sentences.n: αὐτάρ is the epic 'but, and then', where Attic prose would use δέ or ἀλλά. ὁ and τοῖσιν are both pronouns: 'he', the Sun, and 'from them', a dative of the persons deprived with ἀφείλετο, the aorist middle of ἀφαιρέω. ἦμαρ is the epic word for ἡμέρα. With an adjective it makes formulae for a turning point in a life, and νόστιμον ἦμαρ is 'the day of return'. The adjective νόστιμος is formed from νόστος, the word introduced in line 5.

sentences.t: τῶν ἁμόθεν γε, θεά, θύγατερ Διός, εἰπὲ καὶ ἡμῖν.
sentences.l: Of these things, from some point at least, goddess, daughter of Zeus, tell us also.
sentences.i: Of these things, goddess, daughter of Zeus, tell us too, taking them up at whatever point.
sentences.n: τῶν is the pronoun again, a genitive 'of these things'. ἁμόθεν occurs only here in Homer: 'from some point or other', built on an old indefinite ἁμός with the suffix -θεν 'from'. The suffixes -θεν, -θι and -δε mark place from, place where and place to, and recur throughout. εἰπέ is the aorist imperative. καὶ ἡμῖν is 'to us as well', the poet and his audience beside the Muse who knows the whole story. The line closes the proem, which has described the man in ten lines without giving his name.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ ἄλλοι μὲν πάντες, ὅσοι φύγον αἰπὺν ὄλεθρον,
οἴκοι ἔσαν, πόλεμόν τε πεφευγότες ἠδὲ θάλασσαν·
sentences.l:
Then the others all, as many as had fled steep destruction,
at home were, both war having escaped and the sea;
sentences.i: By then all the others, as many as had escaped steep destruction, were at home, safe from both the war and the sea;
sentences.n: ἔνθα is here temporal, 'at that point': this is the moment at which the Muse takes up the story. ἄλλοι μέν is answered by τὸν δέ in line 13. φύγον is unaugmented (Attic ἔφυγον), and ἔσαν is the epic form of ἦσαν. αἰπὺς ὄλεθρος is a formula: αἰπύς means 'steep, sheer', and the usual explanation is that destruction is pictured as a fall from a height. It recurs at 1.37. ἠδέ is an epic 'and'. The perfect participle πεφευγότες describes a lasting state, men who have escaped and remain safe.

sentences.t:
τὸν δ’ οἶον νόστου κεχρημένον ἠδὲ γυναικὸς
νύμφη πότνι’ ἔρυκε Καλυψὼ δῖα θεάων
ἐν σπέσσι γλαφυροῖσι, λιλαιομένη πόσιν εἶναι.
sentences.l:
but him alone, of homecoming in need and of his wife,
a nymph, a lady, was holding back, Calypso, heavenly-one of goddesses,
in hollow caves, yearning for him to be her husband.
sentences.i: but him alone, in want of his homecoming and his wife, the lady nymph Calypso, heavenly even among goddesses, was keeping back in her hollow caves, yearning to have him for her husband.
sentences.n: τόν is the pronoun 'him'. οἶον, with smooth breathing, is 'alone'; οἷον with rough breathing is 'such as', and the two need telling apart. κεχρημένον is the perfect participle of χράομαι and with the genitive means 'in need of'. ἔρυκε is an unaugmented imperfect. πότνια is a title of respect for goddesses and great ladies. The name Καλυψώ is formed from καλύπτω 'hide': she is the Concealer. θεάων is an uncontracted genitive plural (Attic θεῶν), partitive with δῖα. σπέσσι is the dative plural of σπέος 'cave', plural for a single dwelling. λιλαιομένη takes the infinitive.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ ἔτος ἦλθε περιπλομένων ἐνιαυτῶν,
τῷ οἱ ἐπεκλώσαντο θεοὶ οἶκόνδε νέεσθαι
εἰς Ἰθάκην, οὐδ’ ἔνθα πεφυγμένος ἦεν ἀέθλων
καὶ μετὰ οἷσι φίλοισι.
sentences.l:
But when indeed the year came, as the years rolled round,
in which for him the gods had spun-the-thread homeward to return
to Ithaca, not even there was he escaped from trials,
even among his own dear-ones.
sentences.i: But when, as the years came round, the year arrived in which the gods had spun for him his return home to Ithaca, not even there was he clear of trials, not even among his own dear ones.
sentences.n: τῷ is the article-form used as a relative, 'in which'. οἱ is the enclitic dative 'for him' (Attic αὐτῷ) and is very common. ἐπεκλώσαντο is from ἐπικλώθω 'spin': what is fated is a thread the gods spin for a man. οἶκόνδε has the suffix -δε 'towards'. νέεσθαι is uncontracted (Attic νεῖσθαι) and shares its root with νόστος. ἦεν is ἦν; ἀέθλων is Attic ἄθλων; οἷσι is the possessive 'his own'. πεφυγμένος with a genitive is unusual; elsewhere it takes the accusative. As the edition punctuates, the main clause begins at οὐδ’ ἔνθα. Other readers make those words a parenthesis and find the main clause in θεοὶ δ’ ἐλέαιρον.

sentences.t:
θεοὶ δ’ ἐλέαιρον ἅπαντες
νόσφι Ποσειδάωνος·
sentences.l:
And the gods pitied him, all of them,
apart from Poseidon;
sentences.i: The gods all felt pity for him, all but Poseidon;
sentences.n: ἐλέαιρον is the unaugmented imperfect of ἐλεαίρω, an epic by-form of ἐλεέω 'pity'; the object 'him' is left to be understood. The imperfect describes a settled state of feeling. νόσφι with the genitive means 'apart from, except'. Ποσειδάωνος is the uncontracted form of the name, Attic Ποσειδῶνος. The sentence begins in the middle of line 19, after the full stop at φίλοισι, and the exception is held back to the start of the next line.

sentences.t:
ὁ δ’ ἀσπερχὲς μενέαινεν
ἀντιθέῳ Ὀδυσῆι πάρος ἣν γαῖαν ἱκέσθαι.
sentences.l:
but he unceasingly raged
at godlike Odysseus, before he his own land reached.
sentences.i: but he raged without pause against godlike Odysseus, until the man reached his own land.
sentences.n: The hero's name is heard here for the first time, in line 21 and in the dative. ὁ δέ is 'but he', Poseidon. ἀσπερχές is an adverb, 'hotly, without pause'. μενέαινεν is from μενεαίνω 'rage', a verb built on μένος 'force, fury'. πάρος with the infinitive means 'before', like Attic πρίν. ἣν γαῖαν is the possessive ὅς again, 'his own land'. Ὀδυσῆι has a single σ; Homer uses Ὀδυσ- and Ὀδυσσ- as the metre requires. ἀντίθεος 'godlike', literally 'a match for a god', is a general epithet of heroes and is given to Polyphemus at 1.70.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὁ μὲν Αἰθίοπας μετεκίαθε τηλόθ’ ἐόντας,
Αἰθίοπας τοὶ διχθὰ δεδαίαται, ἔσχατοι ἀνδρῶν,
οἱ μὲν δυσομένου Ὑπερίονος οἱ δ’ ἀνιόντος,
ἀντιόων ταύρων τε καὶ ἀρνειῶν ἑκατόμβης.
sentences.l:
But he to the Ethiopians had gone on a visit, who far off are,
the Ethiopians, who in two are divided, the farthest of men,
some where Hyperion sets, the others where he rises,
to partake of a hecatomb of bulls and of rams.
sentences.i: But he had gone to visit the Ethiopians who live far away, the Ethiopians who are divided in two, the farthest of men, some where Hyperion sets and some where he rises, to partake of a hecatomb of bulls and rams.
sentences.n: μετεκίαθε, 'went to visit', has pluperfect sense here. ἐόντας is Attic ὄντας. Αἰθίοπας is repeated at the head of line 23 to carry a description. τοί is the article-form as a relative. δεδαίαται is the third plural perfect passive of δαίω 'divide', with Ionic -αται for -νται. The Ethiopians, whose name the Greeks heard as 'burnt-faces', live at the two edges of the world. ἀντιόων, from ἀντιάω with the vowel stretched out, is here a future participle of purpose, identical in form with the present; it takes the genitive, 'to meet, to partake of'. A ἑκατόμβη is nominally a hundred oxen, in practice any large sacrifice.

sentences.t: ἔνθ’ ὅ γ’ ἐτέρπετο δαιτὶ παρήμενος·
sentences.l: There he was taking-delight, at the feast sitting-by;
sentences.i: There he sat at the feast and took his pleasure;
sentences.n: ἔνθα is local this time, 'there'; at 1.11 it was temporal. ὅ γε is the pronoun, 'he'. ἐτέρπετο keeps its augment: in Homer the augment is optional, and augmented and unaugmented forms stand side by side. δαιτί is the dative of δαίς 'feast, portion'; it can be taken with παρήμενος, the participle of πάρημαι 'sit beside', or with ἐτέρπετο, 'took delight in the feast'. With Poseidon away at the edge of the world, the other gods can meet without him.

sentences.t:
οἱ δὲ δὴ ἄλλοι
Ζηνὸς ἐνὶ μεγάροισιν Ὀλυμπίου ἁθρόοι ἦσαν.
sentences.l:
but the others, now,
in the halls of Olympian Zeus gathered together were.
sentences.i: but the other gods were gathered together in the halls of Olympian Zeus.
sentences.n: οἱ δὲ δὴ ἄλλοι sets the rest of the gods against Poseidon. Ζηνός is a second genitive of Ζεύς, beside Διός in line 10; Homer has both stems. Ζηνός and Ὀλυμπίου belong together, with the words for 'in the halls' enclosed between them. ἐνί is ἐν. μεγάροισιν is a dative plural in -οισι(ν), plural for one house. ἁθρόοι means 'all in a body'; its neuter ἁθρόα comes back at 1.43. ἦσαν here is the same verb as ἔσαν in line 12.

sentences.t: τοῖσι δὲ μύθων ἦρχε πατὴρ ἀνδρῶν τε θεῶν τε·
sentences.l: And among them of speeches made-beginning the father of men and of gods;
sentences.i: Among them the father of men and of gods was first to speak;
sentences.n: τοῖσι is the pronoun in the dative, 'among them'. ἄρχω takes the genitive of the thing begun, so μύθων ἦρχε is 'he began the speaking'. μῦθος in Homer is a speech or a thing said, without the later sense 'myth'. πατὴρ ἀνδρῶν τε θεῶν τε is a fixed title of Zeus that closes the line. 'Father' marks his authority as head of the household of gods and men; he is the actual parent of only some gods and of few men.

sentences.t:
μνήσατο γὰρ κατὰ θυμὸν ἀμύμονος Αἰγίσθοιο,
τόν ῥ’ Ἀγαμεμνονίδης τηλεκλυτὸς ἔκταν’ Ὀρέστης·
sentences.l:
for he remembered in his heart blameless Aegisthus,
whom Agamemnon's-son, the far-famed, had killed, Orestes;
sentences.i: for he called to mind blameless Aegisthus, whom far-famed Orestes, Agamemnon's son, had killed;
sentences.n: ἀμύμων is a stock epithet whose meaning is not known. The old derivation from ἀ- and μῶμος 'blame' gives 'blameless', but it is doubted, and the word seems to mark rank or excellence in a general way. Here it is given to a seducer and murderer. Such an epithet goes with the person's rank, not with the scene, and the translation keeps it every time. μνήσατο is unaugmented and takes the genitive. ῥα is a worn-down ἄρα; ἔκταν’ is ἔκτανε, aorist of κτείνω. Aegisthus took Agamemnon's wife and killed him on his return, and the son avenged the father. That household is the poem's foil for the house of Odysseus.

sentences.t: τοῦ ὅ γ’ ἐπιμνησθεὶς ἔπε’ ἀθανάτοισι μετηύδα·
sentences.l: Of him he, mindful, words among the immortals spoke:
sentences.i: With that man in mind, he spoke among the immortals:
sentences.n: τοῦ is the pronoun, a genitive governed by ἐπιμνησθείς, the aorist passive participle of ἐπιμιμνήσκομαι 'think of'. ὅ γε is 'he', Zeus. ἔπε’ is ἔπεα, the uncontracted accusative plural of ἔπος 'word' (Attic ἔπη). μετηύδα is the imperfect of μεταυδάω 'speak among', with the dative ἀθανάτοισι. A line of this type introduces each speech in this part; the edition ends it with a raised point, and the spoken words begin with the next line. The Greek text prints no quotation marks.

sentences.t: ὢ πόποι, οἷον δή νυ θεοὺς βροτοὶ αἰτιόωνται·
sentences.l: “Ah! how indeed, now, mortals accuse the gods;
sentences.i: “Ah, how mortals do accuse the gods!
sentences.n: ὢ πόποι is an exclamation of surprise or displeasure. Its origin is unknown; an ancient guess that πόποι meant 'gods' is not believed. οἷον is exclamatory, a neuter used as an adverb: 'how!'. νυ is a weak 'now, then'; with ῥα, ἄρ, περ and κε it belongs to a set of small particles that colour a sentence and often resist translation. βροτοί is the poetic word for 'mortals'. αἰτιόωνται is Attic αἰτιῶνται: a contracted -ῶ- has been stretched back out into -όω- to fit the verse. This artificial stretching, called diectasis, recurs often.

sentences.t:
ἐξ ἡμέων γάρ φασι κάκ’ ἔμμεναι, οἱ δὲ καὶ αὐτοὶ
σφῇσιν ἀτασθαλίῃσιν ὑπὲρ μόρον ἄλγε’ ἔχουσιν,
sentences.l:
For from us, they say, evils are; but they themselves too
by their own wanton-follies, beyond portion, pains have,
sentences.i: It is from us, they say, that evils come, when they themselves as well, by their own wanton folly, have pains beyond what was allotted,
sentences.n: ἡμέων is uncontracted ἡμῶν. ἔμμεναι is the epic infinitive of εἰμί (Attic εἶναι); infinitives in -μεναι and -έμεν are regular in Homer. οἱ δέ is the pronoun, 'but they'. καὶ αὐτοί, 'they themselves as well', concedes that some evils do come from the gods. σφῇσιν is from σφός 'their own'. σφῇσιν ἀτασθαλίῃσιν repeats the narrator's phrase at 1.7 about the companions, so that Zeus states as a general rule what the proem gave as one case. μόρος, from μείρομαι 'receive as a share', is a person's portion; ὑπὲρ μόρον is suffering over and above that portion. ἄλγε’ is ἄλγεα.

sentences.t:
ὡς καὶ νῦν Αἴγισθος ὑπὲρ μόρον Ἀτρεΐδαο
γῆμ’ ἄλοχον μνηστήν, τὸν δ’ ἔκτανε νοστήσαντα,
sentences.l:
as even now Aegisthus, beyond portion, of Atreus' son
married the wedded wife, and him he killed when he came home,
sentences.i: just as now Aegisthus, beyond what was allotted, married the wedded wife of the son of Atreus and killed the man when he came home,
sentences.n: Ἀτρεΐδαο is a genitive in -αο of a first-declension masculine (Attic Ἀτρείδου). The patronymic 'son of Atreus' means Agamemnon. γῆμ’ is ἔγημε, unaugmented and elided, the aorist of γαμέω. ἄλοχος, 'one who shares the bed', is a wife. μνηστή means 'wooed and won, lawfully wedded'; it comes from μνάομαι 'woo', the verb of line 39 and the source of μνηστῆρες 'suitors' at 1.91. τὸν δέ is the pronoun, 'and him'. νοστήσαντα is the aorist participle of νοστέω: Agamemnon did reach home, and was killed there.

sentences.t:
εἰδὼς αἰπὺν ὄλεθρον, ἐπεὶ πρό οἱ εἴπομεν ἡμεῖς,
Ἑρμείαν πέμψαντες, ἐύσκοπον ἀργεϊφόντην,
μήτ’ αὐτὸν κτείνειν μήτε μνάασθαι ἄκοιτιν·
sentences.i: though he knew it meant steep destruction, since we ourselves told him beforehand, sending Hermes, the keen-sighted slayer of Argus, that he should neither kill the man nor woo his wife;
sentences.n: εἰδώς takes a direct object: he knew the steep destruction that would follow, the formula of 1.11. πρό … εἴπομεν is tmesis for προείπομεν 'we told beforehand', and οἱ is 'to him'. Ἑρμείας is the epic form of Ἑρμῆς. ἐύσκοπος is 'keen-sighted' or perhaps 'sure of aim'. The meaning of ἀργεϊφόντης is disputed. The ancients explained it as 'slayer of Argus', the many-eyed watchman set over Io, but the formation is irregular for that sense and Homer never tells the story. Others connect it with ἀργός 'bright, swift'. μνάασθαι is μνᾶσθαι with the vowel stretched out. The infinitives with μήτε give the content of the order.

sentences.t:
ἐκ γὰρ Ὀρέσταο τίσις ἔσσεται Ἀτρεΐδαο,
ὁππότ’ ἂν ἡβήσῃ τε καὶ ἧς ἱμείρεται αἴης.
sentences.l:
‘for from Orestes vengeance shall there be for Atreus' son,
whenever he comes of age and for his own land feels longing.’
sentences.i: ‘for vengeance for the son of Atreus will come from Orestes, once he has grown to manhood and feels the longing for his own land.’
sentences.n: With γάρ the report leaves the infinitives of line 39 for Hermes' own words; ὣς ἔφαθ’ Ἑρμείας in line 42 shows that they are direct speech. Ὀρέσταο is another genitive in -αο. As transmitted, the line is metrically irregular at that word: its final -ο has to count as long at the caesura before τίσις, whose ι is short. τίσις 'payment, vengeance' comes from τίνω 'pay', and Ἀτρεΐδαο depends on it as an objective genitive. ἔσσεται is ἔσται. ἱμείρεται is an aorist subjunctive with a short vowel (= ἱμείρηται), beside ἡβήσῃ. ἧς … αἴης is 'his own land', with αἶα a by-form of γαῖα.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφαθ’ Ἑρμείας, ἀλλ’ οὐ φρένας Αἰγίσθοιο
πεῖθ’ ἀγαθὰ φρονέων·
sentences.l:
So spoke Hermes, but not the mind of Aegisthus
did he persuade, though good things intending;
sentences.i: So Hermes said, but for all his good will he did not win over the mind of Aegisthus;
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφατο, 'so he spoke', is the regular formula that closes a speech. ἔφαθ’ is ἔφατο, elided, with τ turned to θ before the rough breathing of Ἑρμείας. The middle of φημί means the same as the active. φρένας, properly the midriff, is the seat of thought and decision. πεῖθ’ is πεῖθε, an unaugmented imperfect: he tried to persuade and did not succeed. ἀγαθὰ φρονέων, 'thinking good things', means 'well disposed towards him'; φρονέων is uncontracted φρονῶν.

sentences.t: νῦν δ’ ἁθρόα πάντ’ ἀπέτισεν.
sentences.l: and now, all together, everything he has paid back.”
sentences.i: and now he has paid the whole debt in one sum.”
sentences.n: ἀπέτισεν is the aorist of ἀποτίνω 'pay back, pay in full'. It has the same root as τίσις in line 40, so the payment Hermes announced has now been made. ἁθρόα is a neuter plural, 'all in a lump', the adjective used of the assembled gods at 1.27. The aorist with νῦν corresponds to an English perfect. The example supports the claim Zeus opened with: the man was warned, and what he suffered he brought upon himself.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα θεά, γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη·
sentences.l: Him then answered the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena:
sentences.i: Then the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena, answered him:
sentences.n: This whole line is a formula of reply: τὸν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα, and then a name with its epithet to fill the rest of the verse. It returns unchanged at 1.80. τόν is the pronoun 'him'. ἠμείβετ’ is ἠμείβετο, the imperfect middle of ἀμείβω 'exchange', in the middle 'answer'. γλαυκῶπις joins γλαυκός 'gleaming', later 'grey-blue', to ὤψ 'eye, face'. An old alternative links it with γλαύξ 'owl', giving 'owl-eyed'. The exact sense is uncertain.

sentences.t: ὦ πάτερ ἡμέτερε Κρονίδη, ὕπατε κρειόντων,
sentences.l: “O father ours, son-of-Cronus, highest of rulers,
sentences.i: “Father of us all, son of Cronus, highest of those who rule,
sentences.n: The line is wholly vocative and is Athena's formal address to Zeus; she uses it again at 1.81. ἡμέτερε 'our' speaks for the assembled gods, though she is also literally his child. Κρονίδη is the vocative of the patronymic Κρονίδης 'son of Cronus'. ὕπατε is a superlative, 'highest'. κρειόντων is the genitive plural of κρείων 'ruling, lord', a participle in form, and is partitive: 'highest among those who rule'.

sentences.t: καὶ λίην κεῖνός γε ἐοικότι κεῖται ὀλέθρῳ·
sentences.l: yes, all too surely that man, at least, in a fitting destruction lies;
sentences.i: yes, that man certainly lies low in a destruction that befits him;
sentences.n: καὶ λίην opens an emphatic agreement, 'yes, and very much so'. λίην is Ionic for λίαν. κεῖνος is ἐκεῖνος. γε limits the agreement to Aegisthus, 'that man at any rate', and prepares the turn to Odysseus at ἀλλά in line 48. ἐοικότι is the perfect participle of ἔοικα, 'fitting, deserved', agreeing with ὀλέθρῳ. κεῖται 'lies' is used of the dead. The line plays on the sound of κεῖνος and κεῖται.

sentences.t: ὡς ἀπόλοιτο καὶ ἄλλος, ὅτις τοιαῦτά γε ῥέζοι·
sentences.l: so may perish any other too, whoever such things should do;
sentences.i: so may anyone else perish who does such things;
sentences.n: The edition prints ὡς without an accent. With the optative of wish ἀπόλοιτο, the aorist middle of ἀπόλλυμι, it is taken here as the adverb 'so, in the same way', which is usually accented ὥς, as at 1.6 and 1.42. Unaccented ὡς can also simply introduce a wish, 'would that'. ὅτις is the epic form of ὅστις 'whoever'. ῥέζοι is optative because the relative clause is drawn into the mood of the wish. ῥέζω is the ordinary epic verb 'do'; at 1.61 it means 'perform a sacrifice'. With γε Athena limits her point to deeds such as these.

sentences.t:
ἀλλά μοι ἀμφ’ Ὀδυσῆι δαΐφρονι δαίεται ἦτορ,
δυσμόρῳ, ὃς δὴ δηθὰ φίλων ἄπο πήματα πάσχει
νήσῳ ἐν ἀμφιρύτῃ, ὅθι τ’ ὀμφαλός ἐστι θαλάσσης.
sentences.l:
But my heart, for Odysseus the wise-minded, is rent,
the ill-fated, who indeed for long, from his dear-ones away, woes suffers
on an island flowed-around, where the navel is of the sea.
sentences.i: but it is for wise-hearted Odysseus that my heart is rent, the ill-fated man, who for so long has suffered woes far from his dear ones, on an island with the sea running all round it, where the navel of the sea is.
sentences.n: δαΐφρονι and δαίεται echo each other. δαίεται may be from δαίω 'divide', as δεδαίαται was at 1.23, or from δαίω 'kindle', giving 'burns'. The meaning of δαΐφρων is doubtful: 'warlike', from δάϊς 'battle', or 'wise, skilled', from δαῆναι 'learn', the sense followed here; a link with δαίω 'kindle' has also been proposed. φίλων ἄπο shows anastrophe: the preposition follows its noun and its accent moves back. With δηθά 'for a long time' the present πάσχει means 'has long been suffering'. ὅθι is 'where' (Attic οὗ), and τε marks a standing fact. ὀμφαλός is a navel, or the boss of a shield: the island lies at the middle of the sea.

sentences.t:
νῆσος δενδρήεσσα, θεὰ δ’ ἐν δώματα ναίει,
Ἄτλαντος θυγάτηρ ὀλοόφρονος, ὅς τε θαλάσσης
πάσης βένθεα οἶδεν, ἔχει δέ τε κίονας αὐτὸς
μακράς, αἳ γαῖάν τε καὶ οὐρανὸν ἀμφὶς ἔχουσιν.
sentences.l:
An island full-of-trees, and a goddess on it has her dwelling,
daughter of Atlas the baleful-minded, who of the sea
entire the depths knows, and holds the pillars himself,
the tall ones, which earth and sky apart hold.
sentences.i: It is a wooded island, and a goddess has her home on it, the daughter of baleful-minded Atlas, who knows the depths of the whole sea and himself holds the tall pillars that hold earth and sky apart.
sentences.n: νῆσος in the nominative restarts the sentence loosely after νήσῳ, with no verb. ἐν is an adverb, 'on it', and δώματα is the object of ναίει: 'she inhabits a house there'. ὀλοόφρονος agrees with Ἄτλαντος. It means 'of destructive mind', from ὀλοός; why Atlas is called so is not known, and an ancient alternative made it 'all-knowing'. ὅς τε and δέ τε have the epic τε of a standing fact. ἀμφὶς ἔχουσιν is either 'keep apart' or 'hold on both sides'. This Atlas knows the sea's depths and has the pillars in his keeping, which differs from the later picture of him bearing the sky on his shoulders.

sentences.t:
τοῦ θυγάτηρ δύστηνον ὀδυρόμενον κατερύκει,
αἰεὶ δὲ μαλακοῖσι καὶ αἱμυλίοισι λόγοισιν
θέλγει, ὅπως Ἰθάκης ἐπιλήσεται·
sentences.i: His daughter keeps the wretched man back as he laments, and she is always enchanting him with soft and coaxing words, so that he will forget Ithaca;
sentences.n: τοῦ is the pronoun as a demonstrative, 'of that one'. κατερύκει is a compound of the verb ἔρυκε used of Calypso at 1.14. δύστηνον ὀδυρόμενον has no noun: 'him, wretched, lamenting'. αἰεί is ἀεί. λόγοισιν is notable, because λόγος is very rare in Homer, whose usual words are μῦθος and ἔπος. θέλγω is the verb of charming and bewitching, by magic or by speech. ὅπως with the future indicative ἐπιλήσεται expresses the end she is working towards, and ἐπιλανθάνομαι 'forget' takes the genitive Ἰθάκης.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Ὀδυσσεύς,
ἱέμενος καὶ καπνὸν ἀποθρῴσκοντα νοῆσαι
ἧς γαίης, θανέειν ἱμείρεται.
sentences.l:
but Odysseus,
eager even the smoke springing-up to glimpse
from his own land, to die is longing.
sentences.i: but Odysseus, in his eagerness to glimpse even the smoke springing up from his own land, longs for death.
sentences.n: The name stands in the nominative for the first time, at the end of line 57 and with double σ. ἱέμενος 'eager' is the participle used of him at 1.6. καί is 'even, no more than': the mere sight of smoke from Ithaca would be enough. ἀποθρῴσκοντα is 'leaping up from', and ἧς γαίης, 'his own land' with the possessive ὅς, is the genitive of the place it rises from. θανέειν is the uncontracted aorist infinitive (Attic θανεῖν). ἱμείρεται is the verb used of Orestes at 1.41, where the longing was for a homeland; here it is for death.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ νυ σοί περ
ἐντρέπεται φίλον ἦτορ, Ὀλύμπιε.
sentences.l:
And not even in you, then,
does it turn, your own heart, Olympian.
sentences.i: Yet not even your own heart, Olympian, turns to take heed.
sentences.n: οὐδέ … περ throws the weight on σοί: 'not even in you', of all the gods. ἐντρέπεται, 'turns towards, pays regard', is a rare verb in Homer. φίλον with ἦτορ means little more than 'your own': φίλος with parts of the body and with kin regularly serves as a possessive. ἦτορ is the word Athena used of her own heart at 1.48. The edition ends the sentence with a full stop after Ὀλύμπιε, and it is taken here as a statement; the same words can also be read as a question.

sentences.l:
Did not Odysseus, then,
beside the Argives' ships gratify you, sacred-rites performing,
in Troy the broad?
sentences.i: Did not Odysseus please you, beside the ships of the Argives, with the sacrifices he offered in the broad land of Troy?
sentences.n: οὐ in a question expects the answer yes. The elided τ’ is unclear: it may be τε, or τοι 'to you', which would supply the dative χαρίζετο needs. νηυσί is the epic dative plural of ναῦς (Attic ναυσί). χαρίζετο is an unaugmented imperfect, 'used to do what pleased you'. ἱερὰ ῥέζων, 'doing sacred things', means offering sacrifice; ῥέζω was plain 'do' at 1.47. Ἀργεῖοι is one of Homer's three names for the Greeks, with Ἀχαιοί and Δαναοί. Τροίῃ εὐρείῃ is the country round Troy. The argument rests on exchange: a man who has sacrificed well has a claim on the god.

sentences.t: τί νύ οἱ τόσον ὠδύσαο, Ζεῦ;
sentences.l: Why, then, him so greatly have you come-to-hate, Zeus?”
sentences.i: Why then, Zeus, have you come to hate him so?”
sentences.n: The line holds a pun on the hero's name. ὠδύσαο is the second person singular aorist middle of ὀδύσσομαι 'be angry at, hate', with the dative οἱ 'at him' and the uncontracted ending -αο (Attic -ω). Its sound repeats Ὀδυσσεύς, the name that closed line 60. The name is thus heard as 'the man of hatred', whether he is the object of the hatred or its source. The verb is found only in the aorist and perfect. τί is 'why', τόσον is an adverb, 'so much', and νυ gives the question an edge of impatience.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη νεφεληγερέτα Ζεύς·
sentences.l: Her answering addressed cloud-gatherer Zeus:
sentences.i: In answer Zeus who gathers the clouds said to her:
sentences.n: This is a second formula of reply, built on a participle and προσέφη: 'answering her, he addressed'. τήν is the pronoun 'her', the object of προσέφη. νεφεληγερέτα is a nominative in short -α, a type found among old titles (ἱππότα, μητίετα) and generally explained as a vocative that came to serve as a nominative. It is compounded of νεφέλη 'cloud' and ἀγείρω 'gather', and names Zeus as the god of the weather. The epithet is fixed and says nothing about his mood in this scene.

sentences.t: τέκνον ἐμόν, ποῖόν σε ἔπος φύγεν ἕρκος ὀδόντων.
sentences.l: “My child, what a word has escaped you, the fence of your teeth.
sentences.i: “My child, what a word is this that has got past the fence of your teeth!
sentences.n: φύγεν, an unaugmented aorist, has two objects, σε and ἕρκος: 'escaped you, that is, the fence of your teeth'. This is the construction of the whole and the part, common in Homer with parts of the body. ποῖον is a reproachful 'what sort of'. ἕρκος ὀδόντων, with a genitive of material, pictures the teeth as a fence that ought to keep a rash word in. The line is a formula of mild rebuke. The edition ends it with a full stop; it is taken here as an exclamation, and it can also be read as a question.

sentences.l:
How could I, then, Odysseus the divine forget,
who surpassing in mind is among mortals, and surpassingly sacrifices to the gods
immortal has given, who the wide sky hold?
sentences.i: How then could I forget divine Odysseus, who is beyond all mortals in mind, and beyond all has given sacrifices to the immortal gods who hold the wide sky?
sentences.n: πῶς ἄν with the optative is a potential question, and ἔπειτα is 'in that case, if things are as you say'. λαθοίμην is the aorist middle of λανθάνω, 'forget', with the genitive; θείοιο is a genitive in -οιο. In περὶ … ἐστί the first περί goes with the verb, 'is superior to', governing βροτῶν, and νόον is an accusative of respect. The second περί is an adverb, 'exceedingly'. ἱρά is a shorter form of ἱερά, the form at 1.61. τοί is the article-form as a relative. Zeus concedes both of Athena's points, the man's mind and his sacrifices.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ Ποσειδάων γαιήοχος ἀσκελὲς αἰεὶ
Κύκλωπος κεχόλωται, ὃν ὀφθαλμοῦ ἀλάωσεν,
ἀντίθεον Πολύφημον, ὅου κράτος ἐστὶ μέγιστον
πᾶσιν Κυκλώπεσσι·
sentences.i: But Poseidon the earth-holder is always stubbornly angry on account of the Cyclops whose eye Odysseus blinded, godlike Polyphemus, whose strength is the greatest among all the Cyclopes;
sentences.n: γαιήοχος is 'earth-holder' or 'earth-carrier'; which verb lies behind -οχος is debated. ἀσκελές is an adverb, 'stubbornly'. Κύκλωπος is a genitive of cause with the perfect κεχόλωται, 'is in a state of anger'. In the relative clause the subject changes to Odysseus without a word to mark it. ὀφθαλμοῦ, a singular, is a genitive of separation with ἀλάωσεν. ἀντίθεον Πολύφημον takes its case from ὅν and not from Κύκλωπος. The epithet is general, like ἀμύμων at 1.29. ὅου is an epic genitive of ὅς (Attic οὗ). Κυκλώπεσσι is a dative plural in -εσσι.

sentences.t:
Θόωσα δέ μιν τέκε νύμφη,
Φόρκυνος θυγάτηρ ἁλὸς ἀτρυγέτοιο μέδοντος,
ἐν σπέσσι γλαφυροῖσι Ποσειδάωνι μιγεῖσα.
sentences.l:
and Thoösa bore him, the nymph,
daughter of Phorcys, of the unharvested salt-sea the lord,
in hollow caves with Poseidon having lain.
sentences.i: the nymph Thoösa bore him, daughter of Phorcys, lord of the sea that yields no harvest, after she lay with Poseidon in the hollow caves.
sentences.n: μιν is the epic accusative pronoun 'him, her, it' (Attic αὐτόν) and is very common. τέκε is the unaugmented aorist of τίκτω. The meaning of ἀτρύγετος is unknown. The ancient explanation is 'unharvested', from τρυγάω 'gather a crop', setting the sea against the grain-giving earth; another connects it with τρύω and makes it 'unwearied'. μέδοντος is a participle, 'ruling', with the genitive. μιγεῖσα, the aorist passive participle of μίγνυμι 'mingle', is the standard expression for sexual union and takes the dative. ἐν σπέσσι γλαφυροῖσι is the phrase used of Calypso's home at 1.15. The name Θόωσα is formed from θοός 'swift'.

sentences.t:
ἐκ τοῦ δὴ Ὀδυσῆα Ποσειδάων ἐνοσίχθων
οὔ τι κατακτείνει, πλάζει δ’ ἀπὸ πατρίδος αἴης.
sentences.l:
From that time, then, Odysseus Poseidon the earth-shaker
does not at all kill, but drives him astray, away from his fatherland.
sentences.i: Ever since then Poseidon the earth-shaker, though he does not kill Odysseus, keeps driving him astray from his native land.
sentences.n: ἐκ τοῦ is 'from that time', or possibly 'for that reason'; the pronoun allows either. οὔ τι is 'not at all'. The present κατακτείνει describes a settled policy: he stops short of killing. πλάζει is the active of πλάγχθη in line 2, so the passive of the proem now has its agent. ἐνοσίχθων, from ἔνοσις 'shaking' and χθών 'earth', names Poseidon as the god of earthquakes; it is his second epithet in this speech, after γαιήοχος at 1.68. αἴης is the by-form of γαίης seen at 1.41.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγεθ’, ἡμεῖς οἵδε περιφραζώμεθα πάντες
νόστον, ὅπως ἔλθῃσι·
sentences.l:
But come, let us here devise, all of us,
his homecoming, how he may come;
sentences.i: But come, let all of us here think out his homecoming, how he is to come;
sentences.n: ἄγεθ’ is ἄγετε, an imperative used as an interjection, 'come now', elided and aspirated before ἡμεῖς. οἵδε points to the gods present in the hall, 'we here'. περιφραζώμεθα is a hortatory subjunctive, 'let us consider from every side'. νόστον, its object, is held over to the head of line 77. ἔλθῃσι is a third singular subjunctive with the ending -ῃσι (Attic ἔλθῃ), a form to expect often. ὅπως ἔλθῃσι, 'how he is to come', depends on the verb of planning and shades into a purpose clause, 'so that he may come'.

sentences.t:
Ποσειδάων δὲ μεθήσει
ὃν χόλον·
sentences.l:
and Poseidon will let go
his own anger;
sentences.i: and Poseidon will let his own anger go;
sentences.n: μεθήσει is the future of μεθίημι 'let go, relax'. ὃν χόλον is the possessive ὅς once more, 'his own anger'; at the head of a line, after a verb, it is easy to mistake for a relative pronoun. χόλος is properly 'gall, bile' and so 'anger', and it is the noun behind κεχόλωται at 1.69. Zeus uses a plain future. He gives Poseidon no order, and states what Poseidon will do once the others are agreed.

sentences.t:
οὐ μὲν γάρ τι δυνήσεται ἀντία πάντων
ἀθανάτων ἀέκητι θεῶν ἐριδαινέμεν οἶος.
sentences.l:
for in no way will he be able, against all
the immortals, in despite of the gods, to keep up strife alone.”
sentences.i: for he will not be able, against all the immortals and in defiance of the gods, to carry on the quarrel alone.”
sentences.n: μέν here is the emphatic particle, a weaker μήν, with no answering δέ. οὔ τι is 'in no way'. ἀντία is an adverb with the genitive, 'against'. ἀέκητι, also with the genitive, is 'against the will of'; ἀθανάτων and θεῶν may be taken together with it, 'against the will of the immortal gods'. ἐριδαινέμεν is an infinitive in -έμεν from ἐριδαίνω 'quarrel', the verb of ἔρις. οἶος 'alone', with smooth breathing as at 1.13, is the last word of line 79, and πάντων 'all' is the last word of line 78.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα θεά, γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη·
sentences.l: Him then answered the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena:
sentences.i: Then the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena, answered him:
sentences.n: The line is identical with 1.44. When the same situation returns, a goddess replying to Zeus, the same verse returns with it. Repetition of this kind is the ordinary method of epic composition and gave a listening audience fixed points to hold on to. ἔπειτα is 'then, next'. θεά and γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη stand in apposition: 'the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena'.

sentences.t: ὦ πάτερ ἡμέτερε Κρονίδη, ὕπατε κρειόντων,
sentences.l: “O father ours, son-of-Cronus, highest of rulers,
sentences.i: “Father of us all, son of Cronus, highest of those who rule,
sentences.n: The address of 1.45 returns word for word, as the reply line 1.44 returned at 1.80. Athena begins both of her speeches to Zeus with this full title. The forms are explained at 1.45.

sentences.t:
εἰ μὲν δὴ νῦν τοῦτο φίλον μακάρεσσι θεοῖσιν,
νοστῆσαι Ὀδυσῆα πολύφρονα ὅνδε δόμονδε,
sentences.l:
if indeed now this is dear to the blessed gods,
that Odysseus the much-minded return home to his own house,
sentences.i: if this is now truly pleasing to the blessed gods, that Odysseus of the many counsels should return to his own home,
sentences.n: φίλον stands without ἐστί; Homer often leaves out the verb 'to be'. μακάρεσσι is a dative plural in -εσσι. τοῦτο looks forward to the accusative and infinitive in the next line, νοστῆσαι Ὀδυσῆα. πολύφρων is the second of three epithets in -φρων that Odysseus receives in this part, after δαΐφρων at 1.48 and before ταλασίφρων at 1.87. In ὅνδε δόμονδε the suffix -δε 'towards' is attached to both the possessive and the noun: 'to his own house'.

sentences.t:
Ἑρμείαν μὲν ἔπειτα διάκτορον ἀργεϊφόντην
νῆσον ἐς Ὠγυγίην ὀτρύνομεν, ὄφρα τάχιστα
νύμφῃ ἐυπλοκάμῳ εἴπῃ νημερτέα βουλήν,
νόστον Ὀδυσσῆος ταλασίφρονος, ὥς κε νέηται·
sentences.l:
Hermes then, the guide, Argeïphontes,
to the island Ogygia let us rouse, so that most quickly
to the fine-plaited nymph he may tell our unerring decision,
the homecoming of Odysseus the enduring-minded, that he is to return;
sentences.i: then let us send Hermes, the guide, the slayer of Argus, speeding to the island of Ogygia, so that he may tell the nymph of the fine-plaited hair, as soon as may be, our unfailing decision: the homecoming of steadfast Odysseus, that he is to return;
sentences.n: The meaning of διάκτορος is unknown; the ancients took it from διάγω as 'conductor' or 'messenger'. For ἀργεϊφόντης see 1.38. ὀτρύνομεν looks like an indicative but is an aorist subjunctive with a short vowel (Attic ὀτρύνωμεν), hortatory. μέν is answered by αὐτὰρ ἐγών in line 88. ὄφρα is the epic 'so that' (Attic ἵνα). νημερτέα, uncontracted, is 'unerring', from νη- 'not' and the root of ἁμαρτάνω. In ὥς κε νέηται, κε is the epic equivalent of ἄν. Ὀδυσσῆος has double σ beside Ὀδυσῆος at 1.65. The island is named here for the first time. ταλασίφρων belongs with τλῆναι 'endure'.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐγὼν Ἰθάκηνδ’ ἐσελεύσομαι, ὄφρα οἱ υἱὸν
μᾶλλον ἐποτρύνω καί οἱ μένος ἐν φρεσὶ θείω,
sentences.l:
but I to Ithaca shall go in, so that his son
I may the more rouse up, and for him put force in his mind,
sentences.i: and I myself will go to Ithaca, to stir his son the more and put fresh force into his spirit,
sentences.n: ἐγών is ἐγώ in the form used before a vowel. Ἰθάκηνδ’ is Ἰθάκηνδε, with the suffix -δε 'to'. ἐσελεύσομαι has ἐς for εἰς. ὄφρα again means 'so that', here with two subjunctives. οἱ occurs twice: the first is 'his', a dative of the possessor with υἱόν and referring to Odysseus; the second is 'in him', the son. θείω is the aorist subjunctive of τίθημι (Attic θῶ). μένος is force, drive, the energy to act. φρεσί is the dative plural of φρένες, the word seen at 1.42. The son is not named in this part.

sentences.t:
εἰς ἀγορὴν καλέσαντα κάρη κομόωντας Ἀχαιοὺς
πᾶσι μνηστήρεσσιν ἀπειπέμεν, οἵ τέ οἱ αἰεὶ
μῆλ’ ἁδινὰ σφάζουσι καὶ εἰλίποδας ἕλικας βοῦς.
sentences.l:
to assembly having called the long-haired-of-head Achaeans,
to all the suitors to give notice, who of his always
thronging sheep slaughter, and rolling-gaited, crumple-horned cattle.
sentences.i: so that he may call the long-haired Achaeans to assembly and give plain notice to all the suitors, who are always slaughtering his thronging sheep and the cattle of rolling gait and crumpled horn.
sentences.n: καλέσαντα is accusative, agreeing with the unexpressed subject of ἀπειπέμεν, although the son was last referred to by the dative οἱ. ἀπειπέμεν, an infinitive in -έμεν, is 'speak out, give notice'. The μνηστῆρες 'suitors' enter the poem here with no explanation; the noun is from μνάομαι, the verb of 1.39. In κάρη κομόωντας, κάρη is an accusative of respect, 'long-haired as to the head', and κομόωντας shows the stretched vowel. μῆλα are sheep and goats, ἁδινά 'close-packed'. εἰλίποδας describes the swinging walk of cattle. ἕλικας is 'twisted', probably of the horns, though the sense is uncertain.

sentences.t:
πέμψω δ’ ἐς Σπάρτην τε καὶ ἐς Πύλον ἠμαθόεντα
νόστον πευσόμενον πατρὸς φίλου, ἤν που ἀκούσῃ,
ἠδ’ ἵνα μιν κλέος ἐσθλὸν ἐν ἀνθρώποισιν ἔχῃσιν.
sentences.l:
And I shall send him to Sparta and to sandy Pylos,
of the homecoming to inquire of his dear father, if somewhere he may hear of it,
and so that good fame among men may hold him.”
sentences.i: And I will send him to Sparta and to sandy Pylos, to find out what he can of his dear father's homecoming, should he chance to hear of it, and so that a good name may be his among men.”
sentences.n: πευσόμενον is the future participle of πυνθάνομαι and expresses purpose: 'to inquire'. It agrees with an unexpressed 'him'. νόστον is the first word of line 94, as it was of lines 77 and 87. ἤν is the epic form of ἐάν, and ἤν που ἀκούσῃ is 'in case he may hear something somewhere'. ἠδέ is 'and'; μιν is 'him'; ἔχῃσιν is a subjunctive in -ῃσι like ἔλθῃσι at 1.77. κλέος, from κλύω 'hear', is what is heard about a man, his reputation, and here it is the subject: fame 'holds' him. The journey has two aims, news of the father and a name for the son.
